title: Personal Project Process Journal: Examples That Work
summary: Personal Project process journal examples show how to record decisions, ATL skills, feedback and reflection for a stronger MYP report with useful models.
body_markdown:
A **Personal Project process journal** captures how your thinking changes while you plan, create, solve problems, and reflect. Useful entries preserve evidence of decisions: what happened, why it mattered, which Approaches to Learning (ATL) skill you applied, and what you decided to do next.


Current IB guidance allows written, visual, audio, or combined documentation. A conventional journal is optional, but documenting your process matters. Follow your school's additional requirements for formats and deadlines.


The examples below follow Maya, a hypothetical MYP student developing food-styling and recipe-testing skills while creating an eight-recipe digital booklet.


### Your process journal checklist


A useful entry includes:


- A date and descriptive title.
- Evidence: a photograph, screenshot, draft, test result, or feedback note.
- An explanation of what happened and why.
- Your decision and its connection to an ATL skill.
- A next step and relevant source details.


One analytical paragraph beside meaningful evidence can be more useful than several descriptive pages. The[MYP Personal Project process journal guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/myp-personal-project-process-journal) provides broader context.


### What MYP guidance expects


The Personal Project includes a process, a product or outcome, and a report. Assessment uses three criteria: Planning, Applying skills, and Reflecting. Each is assessed out of 8, giving a maximum of 24.


Your journal supplies evidence for explaining planning, skill application, product evaluation, and learning. Its value comes from what it reveals about inquiry, action, and reflection. Consult the[MYP Personal Project criteria guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/myp-personal-project-criteria) when deciding what to preserve.


### Personal Project process journal examples


### Defining meaningful goals


Maya initially writes, "I want to make a recipe book because I enjoy cooking." After exploring[realistic Personal Project ideas](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/real-examples-of-ib-myp-personal-projects-for-inspiration) , she develops her direction:


> **12 September, defining goals:** My learning goal is to develop recipe-testing and food-styling skills that make low-waste cooking accessible to beginners. My product will be an eight-recipe digital booklet. Each recipe will use a commonly discarded ingredient and be tested by at least two people.


This separates what Maya wants to learn from what she intends to make. Save the earlier version too, because the comparison shows how her thinking developed.


### Making success criteria useful


Success criteria should describe observable qualities. Maya records her reasoning:


> **19 September, success criteria:** I planned 15 recipes, but I have six weeks for testing. I reduced the target to eight so each recipe can be tested twice and revised. Testers will follow the instructions without verbal help and rate their clarity.


Attach the revised timeline. Together, the entry and evidence explain how available time influenced scope and quality.


A student discovers an early design preserved in a museum of useful mistakes


*An early design sits on display in a museum of useful mistakes.*


### Showing how research changed your work


"I researched photography" records an activity without explaining its influence. Maya adds a comparison:


> **3 October, photography research:** I compared guidance about lighting and tested the same dish beside a window and under the ceiling light. The window photograph showed more accurate color and fewer hard shadows. I will use that location for my next photographs and check whether the results remain consistent.


Save both images and record source details using your school's citation style. The images show the test; the entry explains the decision.


### Demonstrating ATL skills


Naming a skill provides little evidence unless you explain its application:


> **17 October, tester feedback:** Two testers misunderstood "cook until ready." I asked what visual cue would help. Their answers led me to write "cook for 6-8 minutes, until the edges are golden." I applied communication skills by asking focused questions and adapting instructions for beginners.


Select evidence showing the ATL skills with the greatest impact. RevisionDojo's **AI Chat** can clarify categories, while **Tutors** can question unclear reasoning. Keep every account grounded in your actual experience.


### Recording setbacks and revisions


A problem becomes useful evidence when you explain your response:


> **2 November, recipe revision:** The carrot-top sauce tasted bitter in both trials. I researched blanching and tested fewer carrot tops mixed with parsley. Three testers preferred the revision. I added two days to testing and moved cover design later.


Attach quantities, feedback, and the updated plan. This shows how research and testing changed both the product and your schedule.


### Evaluating against criteria


Final entries should acknowledge limitations:


> **28 November, evaluation:** The booklet contains eight recipes, all tested twice. Seven testers completed the recipes without help. However, two found the mobile text small, so accessibility was only partly achieved. I would next investigate a responsive layout.


Connect each judgment to a criterion and evidence. The[Personal Project report structure guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/myp-personal-project-report-structure-explained) helps organize those findings.


### Selecting evidence for your report


Create dated folders for planning, skills, development, feedback, and evaluation. Choose evidence that explains a significant decision, demonstrates skill application, or supports a judgment about your product.


Use a[Personal Project report breakdown](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/myp-personal-project-report-writing-breakdown) and the[report-writing guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-write-myp-personal-project-report) to connect evidence with analysis. Explain what each extract demonstrates rather than expecting an image to speak for itself.


Avoid reconstructing entries at the end. Memory often preserves results while losing alternatives and uncertainty. Undated screenshots, copied research, and skill labels without examples also weaken the record.


### Make the journal useful to your future self


Maya's report becomes easier because she preserved decisions, feedback, revisions, and limitations. Keep entries dated, selective, and analytical, then check the[Personal Project fundamentals](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-is-the-myp-personal-project) .
